vignette: 61-year-old man with a closed left tibial shaft fracture treated in a long-leg cast 8 months ago, now coded ICD-10-CM S82.202K (nonunion). Radiograph sets (AP, lateral, and both obliques) were taken at 4.5 months and again at 8 months after injury, 105 days apart; the radiologist reports no interval change and no bridging callus, i.e., healing has ceased for more than 3 months. The orthopedist orders a noninvasive electrical osteogenic stimulator worn over the cast site.
rationale_note: Tibial nonunion at 8 months; two multi-view radiograph sets 105 days apart show no healing.

vignette: 72-year-old woman with a scaphoid waist fracture of the right wrist sustained 7 months ago and treated in a thumb spica cast; she has had no surgery. Two radiograph sets of the wrist, each with PA, lateral, oblique, and scaphoid views, were obtained exactly 90 days apart before any stimulator treatment. The radiologist's written interpretation states there has been no clinically significant evidence of fracture healing between the two sets. The hand surgeon orders a low-intensity pulsed ultrasonic osteogenic stimulator. She is not using any other bone-growth stimulator.
rationale_note: Ultrasonic for scaphoid nonunion: ultrasonic coverage is not limited to long bones, and since 2005 no prior surgery is needed. Radiograph sets exactly 90 days apart.

vignette: 68-year-old man with a right femoral shaft fracture treated with an intramedullary nail 4 months ago. Radiograph sets with AP and lateral views were taken at 2 weeks and at 4 months after surgery, 95 days apart, and show minimal callus with no progression between them. The orthopedist, concerned about slow healing because the patient smokes, orders a noninvasive electrical osteogenic stimulator now.
rationale_note: Only 4 months since fracture; electrical stimulator nonunion requires >= 6 months.

vignette: 70-year-old woman with a humeral shaft fracture treated in a functional brace 9 months ago. The fracture remains clinically mobile and painful. Two radiograph sets of the humerus, each with AP and lateral views, were taken at 7 months and at 9 months after injury, 60 days apart, and show no healing. No other radiographs exist. Her orthopedist orders a noninvasive electrical osteogenic stimulator.
rationale_note: Fracture 9 months old, but the two radiograph sets are only 60 days apart.

vignette: 66-year-old man with degenerative spondylolisthesis and stenosis scheduled for an instrumented posterolateral fusion from L3 to L5 (three vertebrae: L3, L4, L5). He has had no previous spinal surgery. The spine surgeon orders a noninvasive electrical osteogenic stimulator as an adjunct to the fusion, to begin after surgery.
rationale_note: Boundary: L3-L5 involves exactly 3 vertebrae, which qualifies as multiple level fusion.

vignette: 64-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes who smokes one pack per day, scheduled for her first spinal fusion: a single-level instrumented fusion at L4-L5 (two vertebrae). The surgeon documents that her smoking and diabetes put her at high risk of pseudarthrosis and orders a noninvasive electrical osteogenic stimulator as an adjunct to the fusion surgery.
rationale_note: Single-level L4-L5 fusion (2 vertebrae) and no prior failed fusion. Smoking and diabetes are not NCD criteria.

vignette: 69-year-old man who underwent an L5-S1 fusion exactly 9 months ago; that was his last surgery. CT shows no bridging bone across the fusion level and the surgeon diagnoses a failed fusion (pseudarthrosis). The surgeon orders a noninvasive electrical osteogenic stimulator to treat the failed fusion.
rationale_note: Boundary: failed fusion exactly 9 months after the last surgery (noninvasive electrical).

vignette: 74-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer who sustained a pathologic fracture of the left femoral shaft through a lytic metastasis 10 months ago. Two radiograph sets with multiple views, obtained 120 days apart before any stimulator treatment, carry a radiologist's written interpretation of no clinically significant healing between them. Her oncologist and orthopedist order an ultrasonic osteogenic stimulator for the nonunion.
rationale_note: Tumor-related nonunion (pathologic fracture through metastasis) is excluded, despite proper radiographs.

vignette: 41-year-old man on Medicare through disability with congenital pseudarthrosis of the right tibia (ICD-10-CM Q74.2), with persistent motion at the pseudarthrosis site on radiographs. His orthopedic surgeon plans to implant an invasive (implantable) electrical osteogenic stimulator with a coiled cathode at the pseudarthrosis site during the same operation as a bone graft.
rationale_note: Congenital pseudarthrosis is covered only for the noninvasive device; an invasive stimulator is requested.

vignette: 66-year-old woman with a distal radius shaft fracture 8 months ago treated in a cast. Two radiograph sets of the forearm, each with AP, lateral, and oblique views, were obtained 100 days apart before treatment; the image files are attached to the order. The record contains no written interpretation of either set by any physician. The orthopedist orders an ultrasonic osteogenic stimulator; she uses no other bone-growth device.
rationale_note: Two radiograph sets 100 days apart exist, but no physician written interpretation is in the record.

vignette: 73-year-old man with a left tibial shaft fracture 10 months ago, treated with a cast and then a fracture brace; he has persistent pain and motion at the fracture site. The order for a noninvasive electrical osteogenic stimulator is accompanied by one radiograph set taken last week (AP, lateral, two obliques) showing a persistent fracture line. No other radiographs are in the record.
rationale_note: Fracture 10 months old but the record contains only one radiograph set; serial radiographs not documented.

vignette: 65-year-old man with a tibial shaft nonunion 9 months after injury. Two multi-view radiograph sets taken 110 days apart before treatment have a radiologist's written interpretation of no clinically significant healing between them. He has been using a noninvasive electrical osteogenic stimulator for 6 weeks and will continue it. His surgeon also orders an ultrasonic osteogenic stimulator to be used daily at the same time to speed healing.
rationale_note: Ultrasonic stimulator would be used concurrently with a noninvasive electrical stimulator.
